How the conclusion is weighted

Three quarters on the EBITDA method (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, after a market wage). Appraisal guidance treats those earnings as the main basis for valuing a medical practice. One quarter on the marketplace revenue check at its lower-quartile multiple (0.42). That data is not split by specialty or setting, and this practice has one physician and facility relationships it does not own. The owner-operator method uses the same marketplace data and is shown as a ceiling with no weight. Three quarters of $264,000 plus one quarter of $418,000 is $302,500, rounded to $300,000.
How the range is set

Low case, about $50,000: earnings after a market wage are near zero and a buyer pays for equipment and little else. High case, about $680,000: a buyer assumes a wage near the survey medians ($325,000 base) and counts all $48,000 of stipends, so earnings are about $170,000, and pays 4 times. All three cases assume the owner stays on under contract through a transition.
How this estimate changed

A first version of this page put the value at about $650,000. Two independent reviews found that it used a wage too low for the owner's workload, counted stipends no longer received, and gave half the weight to marketplace sales of ordinary office practices. Both reviews reached about $300,000.
Books
Cash basis and unaudited. No receivables or payables are on the balance sheet, so receivables are added separately below and unpaid bills are not shown.

notes:
**Read this first.** The estimate uses the last twelve months only. That was the best year for earnings before owner pay since 2023: $585,057, against $400,401 in 2025 and $503,428 in 2024. Revenue fell 30% in 2024 and 23% in 2025. On calendar 2025 figures the same method leaves little or nothing after a market wage. A buyer will want proof that the 2026 recovery lasts.

**Three things hold the number down, and all three can be changed.** First, earnings after a market wage are thin: buyers pay for what is left after someone else is paid to do the owner's work, and that is about $88,000, not the $585,000 the books show before the owner is paid. Second, the owner personally produces 76.8% of charges and holds the facility relationships, so most of the goodwill would leave with the owner unless the owner stays on under contract. Third, a buyer's diligence will test the largest revenue lines and the patterns in the risk review (visit levels and place of service). Anything it cannot verify is priced as a discount, an escrow or a reason to walk away. Complete records are what carry care management, the largest single line, through that test. The remaining $32,000 of stipends is pay for the owner's own hours as a medical director. Whoever pays a stipend chooses its own medical director, so a buyer may not count it.

**What moves it up:** at 3 times earnings, each $100,000 of proven yearly earnings adds about $300,000 to an earnings-based offer. A clean outside coding audit, a second and third clinician carrying the census, written facility agreements, monthly accrual-basis statements and two years of growth are what move a buyer from 3 times earnings toward 4 or 5. As an illustration only: revenue of $1.4 million with $330,000 of normalized earnings at 4 to 5 times would be worth about $1.3 to $1.65 million.

**What moves it down:** three things, and each is large next to the earnings a buyer pays for. Care management is the largest single line, about $165,000 a year at October's volume and today's paid rate, so anything that interrupts it matters. The practice cannot yet say how much of the last twelve months' collections it supplied. Visit levels: the risk review puts a finding that half of visits were one level high at $60,000 to $100,000 a year. Billing cost: the third quarter ran at a rate of $107,000 a year against $64,000 for the twelve months. In the low case, earnings after a market wage are near zero and a buyer pays for equipment and little else, about $50,000. Repayment of any past claims found unsupported would come on top and stays with the seller.

**What this means for the owner:** today the practice is worth far more to its owner, about $523,000 a year before the owner's own pay, than to a buyer. The work that raises the price is the same work that makes the practice safer to own: billing the records support, earnings that do not depend on one person, and books a stranger can verify.

inputs: Normalized EBITDA
Multiple applied
2 to 4 times, most likely 3
Evidence

Scope Research, a healthcare deal-data firm, said in 2025 that small primary care practices (revenue under $5 million) usually sell for 3 to 6 times EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization). It shows no individual sales behind that range and notes that most small-practice sales are never announced. No published sale prices were found for one-physician, facility-based practices. The 2 to 4 times used here is a judgment: one turn below that range for a single physician, government fee-for-service payers and facility relationships the practice does not own.
Stretch case

5 to 6 times (about $440,000 to $530,000 on earnings of $88,057) would need a buyer that pays for growth, the owner staying for several years, and documented, transferable relationships. No such buyer has been identified. If the buyer is a hospital, nursing facility operator, home health agency, hospice or other business the owner sends patients to, the federal self-referral and anti-kickback laws in practice hold the price to fair market value, with nothing paid for referrals. For a hospital, the total price must be fixed before the first payment, so an earn-out tied to later revenue does not fit the exception for a one-time sale. Do not plan on this case. Have a healthcare attorney review any offer from a buyer of that kind.
notes: The method a medical group, health system or investor-backed platform would use. It pays for earnings that remain after every clinician, including the owner, is paid a market wage. The price holds only if the owner, or a replacement, works for that wage after the sale. The owner now takes about $415,000 a year in salary and distributions, more than the base wage assumed here. Each $10,000 of yearly pay above that wage lowers the price by about $34,000 at 3 times. A hospital's appraiser will use the pay the hospital actually agrees to, not a survey figure.
